title: ST2 Example 5 — CT4 Style & Calculations
description: 100 marks: deployment capacity, queue growth, reliability and software metrics, plus diagram drawing, matching and scenarios.
scope: L17–L33 and L35 revision, including SOA (L26) and Microservices (L27)
reference: User-supplied actual CT4 assessment export; see ct4-style-analysis.md

questions.prompt: SeatLink has a registration screen, registration state/commands and a domain/service layer. Draw its Model–View–ViewModel architecture on paper or in draw.io. Keep the drawing for self-assessment; the text box can hold a description. Then explain the responsibilities and interactions.

parts.prompt: 1. Draw and label Model, View and ViewModel, with labelled interaction directions. (5 marks)
parts.answer: One valid sketch: View —user commands→ ViewModel; ViewModel —bindable state/change notifications→ View; ViewModel —service/domain operations→ Model; Model —results/state→ ViewModel. The ViewModel exposes presentation state and commands; the Model holds domain data/rules and service access. Allow platform-appropriate data-binding notation.
rubric: 3: three clearly labelled components. 2: correct labelled interactions including View/ViewModel binding and ViewModel/Model interaction.

parts.prompt: 2. Explain each responsibility using the scenario, including where the enrolment-capacity rule belongs. (3 marks)
parts.answer: View renders the registration screen and user interaction. ViewModel exposes selected course, pending/error states and the enrol command. Model/domain service enforces course capacity and maintains registration data; server enforcement remains necessary.
rubric: 1 each: three scenario-grounded responsibilities; capacity rule in domain/model, with ViewModel coordinating rather than replacing it.

questions.prompt: Match each software-quality metric with what it measures. Use each answer once.
options: Relatedness of responsibilities within a module

items.explanation: Each decision adds another independent control-flow route. This metric concerns paths through code; it does not count dependencies or establish correctness.

items.answer: Relatedness of responsibilities within a module
items.explanation: Responsibilities that contribute to one purpose belong together. Cohesion describes relationships inside a module, whereas coupling describes dependencies between modules.
A change to one module may affect another through their dependencies. Coupling therefore describes relationships across boundaries, rather than the focus of one module.
This combines several measures into a maintainability indicator. It is neither a raw defect count nor proof that a module is easy to change.

questions.prompt: SeatLink is preparing for peak registration. Use the original deployment/capacity diagram below. A student is active when they generate requests at the stated fixed cadence; they may have overlapping requests. All capacities are aggregate hard limits with perfect load balancing. Use the fluid steady-state approximation: resource throughput = concurrent slots / seconds held. One API slot is occupied for the entire request duration. Every API pod eagerly reserves its full primary pool; there is no external pooler. All non-primary pools are shared aggregate limits as shown. The enrol/booking duration already includes broker-confirm waiting. No other bottlenecks, retries or failures occur. The broker starts empty, has enough storage and applies no backpressure; consumers sustain their stated rate. The queue is not required to stay bounded until part 7. Calculate theoretical upper bounds, not operational targets with safety headroom. Show formulas, substitutions and units.

parts.prompt: 1. Counting only the web tier, how many active students can be served? (3 marks)
parts.answer: Web throughput = 600 requests/s. Each student produces 1/5 requests/s. Active students = 600 × 5 = 3,000. This is only a web-tier upper bound.
rubric: Automatic result marks: 3. Each field is marked independently using the disclosed values/tolerances; method in the working box is retained for review and does not receive automatic credit.

checks.explanation: Multiply instance count by each instance’s sustainable request rate.
Each student emits one request every 5 seconds, so multiply web requests/s by 5.

parts.prompt: 2. What is the largest total API pod count allowed by primary connection reservations? (3 marks)
parts.answer: Usable connections = 140 − 20 = 120. Maximum pods = floor(120 / 12) = 10; the eleventh would reserve 132 > 120.
rubric: Automatic result marks: 3. Each field is marked independently using the disclosed values/tolerances; method in the working box is retained for review and does not receive automatic credit.

checks.explanation: Subtract reserved administrative connections from the primary connection limit.
Divide usable connections by the full reserved per-pod pool and floor to a whole pod.

parts.prompt: 3. At that pod count, what is the maximum enrol throughput? Compare API slots, primary transactions, fee checks and broker confirms. Reads are absent for this part. (3 marks)
parts.answer: API slots = 400 / 0.400 = 1000 enrols/s. Primary connections = 120 / 0.100 = 1200 transactions/s. Fee checks = 40 / 0.250 = 160/s. Confirms = 500/s. Web = 600/s. Minimum = 160 enrols/s, limited by fee checks. Database-only transaction capacity is not end-to-end capacity.
rubric: Automatic result marks: 3. Each field is marked independently using the disclosed values/tolerances; method in the working box is retained for review and does not receive automatic credit.

checks.explanation: Divide all API request slots by total write-request occupancy in seconds.
Divide usable primary connections by transaction hold time in seconds.
Divide check-service concurrency by one check’s duration in seconds.
The diagram gives this aggregate confirmation limit directly.
Take the smallest end-to-end bound, including the web tier.
The external check bound is lower than the API, primary, web and confirmation bounds.

parts.prompt: 4. What is the replica read throughput bound, and the corresponding total request bound under the stated read/write mix? (3 marks)
parts.answer: 60 / 0.050 = 1,200 reads/s. Because reads are 75% of requests, total request bound = 1,200 / 0.75 = 1,600 requests/s.
rubric: Automatic result marks: 3. Each field is marked independently using the disclosed values/tolerances; method in the working box is retained for review and does not receive automatic credit.

checks.explanation: Use replica connection hold time, not the complete read duration.
Divide the read rate by the read fraction because only that fraction of total traffic uses this path.

parts.prompt: 5. Across the complete synchronous request path at the part-2 pod count, how many active students can be supported? Compare the web, API, read, write/check and confirm limits. (3 marks)
parts.answer: Mean API occupancy = 0.75 × 0.06 + 0.25 × 0.4 = 0.145 s/request; API bound = 400 / 0.145 = 2758.62 total requests/s. Other total-request bounds: web 600; replica 1600; primary 4800; fee 640; broker confirms 2000. Minimum = 600 requests/s. Active students = 600 × 5 = 3,000. Web is the bottleneck; enrolments occur at 150/s.
rubric: Automatic result marks: 3. Each field is marked independently using the disclosed values/tolerances; method in the working box is retained for review and does not receive automatic credit.

checks.explanation: Weight each full request duration by its share of traffic.
Divide all API slots by weighted occupancy; two decimal places are sufficient.
The smallest mix-adjusted total bound is 600 requests/s; multiply by the 5-second cadence.
Compare every limit in total requests/s, rather than comparing a read rate directly with a write rate.

parts.prompt: 6. At the part-5 load, how many email messages are waiting after 10 minutes? Start with an empty broker. (3 marks)
parts.answer: Arrival rate = 600 × 0.25 = 150 messages/s. Net queue growth = 150 − 100 = 50 messages/s. Elapsed time = 10 × 60 = 600 seconds. Waiting messages = max(0, 50 × 600) = 30,000. Consumer throughput is distinct from broker-confirm throughput.
rubric: Automatic result marks: 3. Each field is marked independently using the disclosed values/tolerances; method in the working box is retained for review and does not receive automatic credit.

checks.explanation: Multiply completed total requests/s by the write fraction; each write emits one message.
Subtract 100 consumer messages/s, then multiply net growth by 600 seconds.

parts.prompt: 7. What is the largest active-student load for which the email queue does not grow indefinitely? (3 marks)
parts.answer: For a bounded queue in this deterministic model, message arrival must be ≤ 100/s. Total request bound = 100 / 0.25 = 400/s. Other bounds are higher. Active students ≤ 400 × 5 = 2,000. Equality is the theoretical limit; real variable workloads need spare capacity.
rubric: Automatic result marks: 3. Each field is marked independently using the disclosed values/tolerances; method in the working box is retained for review and does not receive automatic credit.

checks.explanation: For a bounded queue, sustained arrivals cannot exceed sustained consumer processing.
Divide the publication/consumer rate by the write fraction.
Multiply queue-stable total rate by cadence and verify that other resource bounds are higher.

parts.prompt: 8. Double the number of web instances while retaining every other limit. Calculate the new supported student count and identify the new limiting resource. (3 marks)
parts.answer: The web limit becomes 1,200 requests/s. Fee checks still cap enrolments at 160/s, hence total traffic at 160 / 0.25 = 640 requests/s. Replica permits 1,600 total requests/s; API slots permit 400 / 0.145 ≈ 2,758.62 total requests/s. New capacity = 640 × 5 = 3,200 active students, limited by the fee service. Extra web instances do not remove that dependency limit.
rubric: Automatic result marks: 3. Each field is marked independently using the disclosed values/tolerances; method in the working box is retained for review and does not receive automatic credit.

checks.prompt: Active students after the proposed change
checks.explanation: Recompute the changed resource and take the minimum of all unchanged and changed bounds.
After the change, fee throughput allows only 640 total requests/s.

questions.prompt: Match each isolation-stack element with its defining role. Use each answer once.
options: Execution flow within a process sharing its address space
Process isolation and resource controls using the host kernel
Layer creating and managing virtual machines
Hardware providing processor, memory and devices

items.answer: Hardware providing processor, memory and devices
items.explanation: The host is the actual machine supplying CPU, memory and devices. Virtual machines and containers consume these resources through software layers.

items.answer: Layer creating and managing virtual machines
items.explanation: A hypervisor provides virtual hardware and manages guest virtual machines. It differs from container isolation, which normally shares the host kernel.

items.answer: Process isolation and resource controls using the host kernel
items.explanation: Namespaces, resource controls and related restrictions isolate processes while they use the host kernel. A container does not normally contain a separate booted guest kernel.

items.answer: Execution flow within a process sharing its address space
items.explanation: Threads are execution flows within a process and share that process’s address space. They are not independent machines or container runtimes.

questions.prompt: A module has length 40, fan-in 3 and fan-out 4. Its application contains 18 confirmed defects in 9 KLOC. A separate single-entry, single-exit function has three binary decisions: one loop and two if-statements (no compound Boolean predicates). Use information-flow complexity = length × (fan-in × fan-out)^2; defect density = defects / KLOC; cyclomatic complexity = binary decisions + 1.

parts.prompt: 1. Calculate original information-flow complexity. (2 marks)
parts.answer: 40 × (3 × 4)² = 40 × 144 = 5,760. Square the product of fan-in and fan-out.
rubric: Automatic result marks: 2. Each field is marked independently using the disclosed values/tolerances; method in the working box is retained for review and does not receive automatic credit.

checks.explanation: Multiply length by the square of fan-in × fan-out; do not square length.

parts.prompt: 2. Fan-out is reduced to 2, with length and fan-in unchanged. Calculate the new score and percentage reduction. Explain one limit of this result. (2 marks)
parts.answer: New score = 40 × (3 × 2)² = 1440. Reduction = (5760 − 1440) / 5760 × 100% = 75.00%. This predictor alone does not prove correctness or maintainability; functional checks and contextual review remain necessary.
rubric: Automatic result marks: 1.5. Each field is marked independently using the disclosed values/tolerances; method in the working box is retained for review and does not receive automatic credit.
Self-assessed reasoning: 0.5 marks. Explain why the metric does not prove correctness/maintainability.

checks.explanation: Keep length and fan-in unchanged; substitute the new fan-out.
Use (old − new) / old × 100; round to two decimals.

parts.prompt: 3. Calculate defect density and give the unit. (2 marks)
parts.answer: 18 / 9 = 2 defects/KLOC. The KLOC denominator is already in thousands of lines; do not divide the result by another thousand.
rubric: Automatic result marks: 2. Each field is marked independently using the disclosed values/tolerances; method in the working box is retained for review and does not receive automatic credit.

checks.explanation: Divide defect count by size already expressed in KLOC; do not divide again by 1,000.

parts.prompt: 4. Calculate cyclomatic complexity and state what it counts. (2 marks)
parts.answer: 3 + 1 = 4. It counts linearly independent control-flow paths under the stated simplified binary-decision model; it is different from information-flow complexity.
rubric: Automatic result marks: 1. Each field is marked independently using the disclosed values/tolerances; method in the working box is retained for review and does not receive automatic credit.
Self-assessed reasoning: 1 marks. Explain that cyclomatic complexity counts independent control-flow paths.

checks.explanation: Under the stated binary-decision model, add one to the decision count.

questions.prompt: A test team holds expected traffic for 48 hours to detect increasing memory use and resource leaks. What is the most specific testing category?
questions.explanation: The long duration is intended to expose accumulation; a spike concerns an abrupt change in load.
optionExplanations: Unit tests check a small isolated unit; the scenario describes sustained whole-service traffic.
Spike testing observes abrupt changes, not accumulation over 48 hours.
Soak testing sustains load long enough for memory/resource accumulation to appear.
Code review inspects an implementation; it does not execute a long-running workload.

questions.prompt: Match each term with its precise meaning. Use each answer once.
options: Capabilities exposed through agreed service boundaries
Caller obligation before invoking an operation

items.answer: Caller obligation before invoking an operation
items.explanation: A precondition must hold before the provider is obliged to perform the operation. For example, the caller may need to supply a valid booking identifier.
A postcondition states the result or invariant guaranteed after successful completion when preconditions hold. It is a provider obligation, not a prerequisite.
Changing fields, types or meaning can break consumers. Versioning, compatibility rules and migration allow interfaces/messages to change deliberately.

items.answer: Capabilities exposed through agreed service boundaries
items.explanation: Business capabilities are accessed through agreed service contracts. The concept is about capability boundaries and interfaces, not simply putting every class in a separate process.

questions.prompt: A signed-in student can alter a registration ID in the URL and read another student’s record. Select all statements supported by this scenario. The stated practice negative-marking rule applies.
options: Authentication alone does not enforce per-record authorisation.
Hiding the ID field in the browser is a sufficient fix.
The server must check access to the requested record.
An automated two-account access test can check this regression.
Using HTTPS by itself prevents this access flaw.
A least-privilege review should include record ownership rules.
questions.explanation: The failure is object-level authorisation. B and E do not enforce who may access a record; A, C, D and F address the evidenced defect.
optionExplanations: A valid login establishes identity but does not establish permission to view every record.
A user can bypass the interface and send a modified request directly.
Access must be checked on the server against the particular record and requesting user.
Use two separate users and verify that one cannot access the other’s private record.
HTTPS protects traffic in transit; it does not decide which authenticated user owns a record.
Least privilege should restrict access to the appropriate owned or authorised records.

questions.prompt: During a SeatLink demo, the presenter speaks toward the monitor, silently waits for a 40-second job, then rapidly clicks through pages without explaining why a student needs them. Identify three distinct problems. For each, explain its effect on assessment and give one concrete correction.

parts.prompt: Give three problem/effect/correction triples. (6 marks)
parts.answer: 1. Speaking to the monitor makes the explanation hard to hear and weakens engagement: face the panel, project clearly and keep the display visible. 2. Silent waiting obscures engineering: explain worker execution, processing state and an implementation trade-off, or demonstrate another feature while the job runs. 3. Uncontextualised clicking forces the panel to infer intent: introduce the student’s goal, explain each meaningful state transition and show its outcome.
rubric: 2 each for three distinct triples: 0.5 problem, 0.5 effect, 1 concrete correction.

questions.prompt: Match each reliability term to the course definition. Use each answer once.

items.explanation: Sum operating intervals and divide by observed failures. Repair intervals are excluded from the operating-time numerator.
Sum restoration intervals and divide by completed restorations. It measures recovery duration, rather than time spent operating successfully.
For this course, MTBF includes the mean operating interval and mean repair interval: MTTF + MTTR. Do not substitute it directly for uptime in the availability numerator.

questions.prompt: An HPC service completes three operating/failure/repair cycles. It runs for 180 hours, then takes 6 hours to restore; runs for 240 hours, then takes 10 hours to restore; and runs for 300 hours, then takes 8 hours to restore. Observation stops when the third restoration completes. All downtime is counted in the repair intervals. Use the course convention MTBF = MTTF + MTTR and Availability = MTTF / (MTTF + MTTR) × 100%. Show working. Round percentages to two decimal places; keep full precision in intermediate calculations.

parts.prompt: 1. Calculate MTTF and MTTR in hours. (4 marks)
parts.answer: Total operating time = 180 + 240 + 300 = 720 h; three failures, so MTTF = 720 / 3 = 240 h. Total repair time = 6 + 10 + 8 = 24 h; MTTR = 24 / 3 = 8 h.
rubric: Automatic result marks: 4. Each field is marked independently using the disclosed values/tolerances; method in the working box is retained for review and does not receive automatic credit.

checks.explanation: Convert operating intervals to hours, sum them and divide by three failures.
Sum restoration durations only and divide by three restorations.

parts.prompt: 2. Calculate MTBF and availability. (3 marks)
parts.answer: MTBF = 240 + 8 = 248 h. Availability = 240 / 248 × 100% = 96.77%. This agrees with total uptime / total observed cycle time.
rubric: Automatic result marks: 3. Each field is marked independently using the disclosed values/tolerances; method in the working box is retained for review and does not receive automatic credit.

checks.explanation: Use the stated course convention: MTTF + MTTR.
Divide mean uptime by mean uptime plus mean repair time, then multiply by 100; two decimal places.

parts.prompt: 3. Recovery automation changes MTTR to 2 hours while MTTF stays unchanged. Calculate availability and state whether fewer failures have been demonstrated. (3 marks)
parts.answer: Availability = 240 / (240 + 2) × 100% = 99.17%. Fewer failures have not been demonstrated: mean operating time is unchanged; restoration is faster. Availability improves through reduced downtime.
rubric: Automatic result marks: 2. Each field is marked independently using the disclosed values/tolerances; method in the working box is retained for review and does not receive automatic credit.
Self-assessed reasoning: 1 marks. Explain that faster restoration improves availability without demonstrating fewer failures.

checks.explanation: Keep MTTF at 240 h; substitute the faster MTTR in the denominator; two decimal places.

parts.prompt: 4. With the original MTTF, what is the maximum MTTR meeting availability ≥ 99.5%? Give hours to four decimal places and approximate minutes. Treat the unrounded value as the acceptance limit. (2 marks)
parts.answer: 240 / (240 + r) ≥ 0.995; hence r ≤ 240 × (1 / 0.995 − 1) = 1.2060 h ≈ 72.36 minutes. The exact unrounded expression is the limit; a rounded-up repair target could narrowly fail it.
rubric: Automatic result marks: 2. Each field is marked independently using the disclosed values/tolerances; method in the working box is retained for review and does not receive automatic credit.

checks.explanation: Rearrange A = 240 / (240 + r): r ≤ 240 × (1/A − 1). Enter four decimal places.
Multiply the unrounded hour limit by 60; two decimal places.

questions.prompt: Match each code-quality practice with its most direct outcome. Use each answer once.
options: Records non-obvious reasons for design decisions
Keeps a component focused on one reason to change
Communicates the purpose of variables and operations

items.answer: Communicates the purpose of variables and operations
items.explanation: A useful name reveals intent and reduces the amount of surrounding code a reader must inspect. It helps comprehension but does not replace tests.

items.answer: Keeps a component focused on one reason to change
items.explanation: Responsibilities that change for different reasons are separated. This limits unrelated change impact and makes focused testing and maintenance easier.
Validate assumptions and handle unexpected inputs or states deliberately so they do not become uncontrolled failures. Silently ignoring every error is not defensive behaviour.

items.answer: Records non-obvious reasons for design decisions
items.explanation: Code often shows what happens, but not why a trade-off was chosen. A rationale comment records the reason rather than repeating an obvious statement.

questions.prompt: Read this self-contained UML deployment model. Boxes show device nodes, contained execution environments and deployed artifacts; connecting lines are communication paths. In text, the browser communicates with the API host over HTTPS/TLS 1.3, and the API host communicates with the database host over PostgreSQL wire protocol/TCP 5432. Answer from the labels rather than guessing a technology.

parts.prompt: 1. Is this a coherent deployment model? Give one diagram-based reason. (2 marks)
parts.answer: Yes. It shows artifacts located in execution environments on device nodes and labelled communication paths between deployed nodes. Naming a technology alone would not establish the deployment placement.
rubric: Automatic result marks: 1. Each field is marked independently using the disclosed values/tolerances; method in the working box is retained for review and does not receive automatic credit.

checks.explanation: The model places artifacts inside execution environments on devices and labels communication paths.

parts.prompt: 2. Identify the backend technology and database schema. (2 marks)
parts.answer: Backend: Node.js. Main schema: Registration. PostgreSQL is the database engine, not the schema name.
rubric: Automatic result marks: 2. Each field is marked independently using the disclosed values/tolerances; method in the working box is retained for review and does not receive automatic credit.

parts.prompt: 3. Classify registration.js and identify the environment hosting it. (2 marks)

rubric: Automatic result marks: 2. Each field is marked independently using the disclosed values/tolerances; method in the working box is retained for review and does not receive automatic credit.

The deployed file sits in the named runtime within the API host.

parts.prompt: 4. Name the database communication protocol/port, and explain why drawing only the software classes would not answer a deployment question. (2 marks)
parts.answer: PostgreSQL wire protocol over TCP port 5432. A class diagram shows software types and relationships; a deployment diagram additionally locates runtime artifacts on execution environments/devices and shows communication paths.
rubric: Automatic result marks: 1. Each field is marked independently using the disclosed values/tolerances; method in the working box is retained for review and does not receive automatic credit.

questions.prompt: A team develops SeatLink with generated code and copied interface widgets. It changes a service response from numeric courseId to an incompatible nested object without telling consumers. Students sometimes submit twice because the UI gives no pending state. The deployment pipeline runs only lint checks, and the team proposes splitting every module into a separately deployed service next week to “make it scalable”.

parts.prompt: 1. Give one design-system practice and one user-feedback improvement, explaining the benefit of each. (2 marks)
parts.answer: Adopt documented reusable form/validation components and common interaction rules to reduce inconsistent interfaces. Disable or safely handle repeat submission while showing pending/success/failure state, so students understand progress; server idempotency is still needed for retries.
rubric: 1: reusable design-system practice with benefit. 1: specific feedback improvement with benefit.

parts.prompt: 2. Propose three CI/DevSecOps checks tied to the faults in this scenario. (3 marks)
parts.answer: Add consumer/provider contract compatibility tests for the changed response; an integration test verifying duplicate-safe enrolment and real boundary behaviour; and security/static/dependency checks plus review of generated code before release. Fail the pipeline on stated violations and retain evidence.
rubric: 1 each: three distinct scenario-linked checks. Accept accessibility/UI regression checks if well justified; lint alone does not prove these behaviours.

parts.prompt: 3. Evaluate the proposed microservices split; give one alternative and a trade-off. (2 marks)
parts.answer: Splitting every module introduces distributed communication, data and release costs without demonstrating a measured bottleneck or cohesive service boundaries. A modular monolith with targeted worker/service extraction can preserve simpler transactions while scaling measured hotspots; independent deployment is limited until extraction. Accept a selective microservices proposal with ownership and operations support.
rubric: 1: causal critique. 1: suitable alternative and relevant trade-off.

parts.prompt: 4. State one domain invariant and one review obligation for generated code. (2 marks)
parts.answer: Invariant: successful active enrolments must not exceed course capacity, enforced atomically on the server. Generated code must be understood and checked against requirements, security and tests by the owning team; plausible output is not evidence of correctness.
rubric: 1: grounded domain invariant. 1: concrete generated-code review responsibility.

Suggested practice time: 150 minutes. Enter numeric answers without units (units are on each label). Percentages: two decimal places, accepted within 0.005 percentage points; MTTR target hours: four decimals, within 0.00005 h. Preserve full precision while working. Keep drawings on paper or in draw.io; this page does not upload images.
